'''Robert John Aitken''' (born 4 September 1947)<ref name=":3">{{cite web |title= Aitken RJ |url=https://id.loc.gov/authorities/names/n81130457.html | publisher = The Library of Congress | work = Linked Data Service, LC Name Authority File (LCNAF)|access-date=5 January 2021}}</ref> is an Anglo-Australian reproductive biologist, widely known for identifying oxidative stress as a significant contribution to infertility and its actions on human sperm function. He also made substantial contributions to clinical practice translation in male reproductive health, notably the development of new contraceptive vaccine.

He was born in Bath, England but moved to Australia in 1997, where he took Chair of Biological Sciences at the University of Newcastle,<ref name=":2" /> then nominated to Pro-Vice-Chancellor of the Faculty of Health and Medicine and Laureate Professor of Biological Sciences at the [[University of Newcastle (Australia)|University of Newcastle]] since 2013.<ref name=":1" /> He is currently Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]],<ref name=":8">{{cite web|title=Professor Robert John Aitken FRSE – The Royal Society of Edinburgh|url=https://www.rse.org.uk/fellow/john-aitken/|access-date=20 March 2018|work=The Royal Society of Edinburgh}}</ref> the [[Australian Academy of Science]]<ref name=":9">{{cite web|title=Professor John Aitken|url=https://www.science.org.au/professor-john-aitken|access-date=20 March 2018|work=Australian Academy of Science|archive-date=26 June 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180626001918/https://www.science.org.au/professor-john-aitken|url-status=dead}}</ref> and the [[Australian Academy of Health and Medical Sciences]],<ref name=":10">{{cite web|title=Fellowship|url=http://www.aahms.org/fellowship/|access-date=25 June 2018|work=AAHMS – Australian Academy of Health and Medical Sciences|language=en-AU}}</ref> a former president of the International Society of Andrology.<ref name=":11">{{Cite web|title=ISA Officers {{!}} International Society of Andrology|url=https://www.andrology.org/isa-officers/|access-date=26 May 2021|language=en-US}}</ref> Aitken also founded and directed the Priority Research Centre in Reproduction at the University of Newcastle, where he and his colleagues work on a broad spectrum of reproductive issues from conception to parturition.

Aitken has received many honours for his contributions to science throughout his career, including the Carl G. Hartman Award and the 2012 NSW Scientist. 
Aitken is the most cited author of several biology journals, particularly in the field of [[Andrology]]: [[Reproduction]], [[Molecular Human Reproduction]], [[International Journal of Andrology]], [[Journal of Andrology]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://exaly.com/author/6775078/r-j-aitken/rankings |title=R. J. Aitken citation rankings |website=Exaly | access-date=2022-06-24}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Aitken was born in [[Bath, Somerset|Bath]],<ref name=":0" /> in [[England]], on 4 September 1947.<ref name=":3" /> Born into a family of real estate agents in [[Devon]], he attended [[The Park Community School|Barnstaple Boys Grammar School]],<ref name=":0" /> but quit at the age of 16 to follow his parents' footsteps and become an estate agent.<ref name=":0">{{cite web| vauthors = Phillips N |date=18 January 2013|title=Using science to give birth to a better world|url=https://www.smh.com.au/healthcare/using-science-to-give-birth-to-a-better-world-20130118-2cykz.html|access-date=16 May 2021| work = The Sydney Morning Herald|language=en}}</ref> After six months of selling houses to the semi-rural residents of Barnstaple, Aitken decided to return to school.<ref name=":0" /> He then re-enrolled at his former school to study art, English, and geography, but they were all full, so he had no choice but to study chemistry, botany, and zoology, despite his initial intention to avoid science.<ref name=":0" />

Aitken graduated from the [[University College London|University of London]], where he received a [[Bachelor of Science|Bachelor of Science (Special Honours)]] in 1967.<ref name=":1">{{cite web|last=ORCID|title=Robert John Aitken (0000-0002-9152-156X)|url=https://orcid.org/0000-0002-9152-156X|access-date=21 April 2021| work = Open Researcher and Contributor ID (ORCID) |language=en}}</ref> While at university, he studied [[zoology]], specifically embryology,<ref name=":12">{{cite web| vauthors = Phillips N |date=14 November 2012|title=Thinking about sex all the time becomes an honour|url=https://www.smh.com.au/technology/thinking-about-sex-all-the-time-becomes-an-honour-20121114-29cgy.html|access-date=16 May 2021| work = The Sydney Morning Herald|language=en}}</ref> which made him interested in [[reproductive biology]], prompting him to pursue a [[Master's degree]] in Embryology and Mammalian Reproduction from the [[University College of North Wales]] in 1969.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{cite journal | vauthors = Aitken RJ | title = Lessons learned in Andrology: revelations on a road less traveled | journal = Andrology | volume = 3 | issue = 5 | pages = 805–8 | date = September 2015 | pmid = 26311338 | doi = 10.1111/andr.12087 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

He continued his post-graduate studies focusing on wild animal reproduction in Veterinary Clinical Studies at the [[University of Cambridge]] under Professor [[Roger Valentine Short|Roger Short]]'s supervision.<ref name=":2" />

=== First scientific papers ===
In 1971, Aitken's first paper, "Ultrastructural changes in the uterine glands of the Roe deer during delayed implantation” was published in the [[The Journal of Physiology|Journal of Physiology]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Aitken RJ, Burton J, Hawkins J, Kerr-Wilson R, Short RV, Steven DH | title = Histological and ultrastructural changes in the blastocyst and reproductive tract of the roe deer, Capreolus capreolus, during delayed implantation | journal = Journal of Reproduction and Fertility | volume = 34 | issue = 3 | pages = 481–93 | date = September 1973 | pmid = 4354893 | doi = 10.1530/jrf.0.0340481 | doi-access = free }}</ref> After 4 years working with Dr Roger Short, Aitken completed his thesis,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Aitken RJ | title = Delayed implantation in roe deer (Capreolus capreolus) | journal = Journal of Reproduction and Fertility | volume = 39 | issue = 1 | pages = 225–33 | date = July 1974 | pmid = 4851283 | doi = 10.1530/jrf.0.0390225 | doi-access = free }}</ref> and received a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] for research on [[Reproductive system|reproductive study]] in roe deer from the University of Cambridge in 1973.<ref name=":1" />

== Scientific career ==

=== 1973–1976: first start on research career ===
After Cambridge, Aitken started a postdoctoral position at the [[University of Edinburgh]]'s Institute of Animal Genetics,<ref name=":1" /> working collaboratively with [[Anne McLaren]], a graduate from the [[University of Oxford]].<ref name=":2" />  However, for the first 12 months at Edinburgh, he had not done any outstanding research due to transformations in study models from [[Descriptive research|descriptive]] on wild animals to mechanistic approaches using the [[mouse]], as well as changes in laboratories.<ref name=":2" /> Despite initial difficulties, he became familiar with new study models of [[in vitro fertilisation]] and [[embryo transfer]] in the second year.<ref name=":2" /> In later years, combining these techniques with [[Gel electrophoresis of proteins|electrophoretic analysis of proteins]], his publication rate rose dramatically<ref name=":2" /> and was being cited by other scientists at that time.<ref>{{cite web|title=Scopus preview – Scopus – Welcome to Scopus|url=https://www.scopus.com/home.uri|access-date=19 May 2021|website=www.scopus.com}}</ref>

==== WHO mission ====
In late 1975, Aitken was invited to study problems associated with fertility regulation at the [[World Health Organization|World Health Organisation (WHO)]]'s Human Reproduction Unit in [[Geneva]].<ref name=":1" /> As consulting scientists of WHO, he and [[Mike Harper (scientist)|Mike Harper]]<ref name=":2" /> conducted several reviews on fertility control strategies, which help prevent or disrupt implantation.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Aitken RJ, Harper MJ | title = New methods for the regulation of implantation | language = English | journal = Contraception | volume = 16 | issue = 3 | pages = 227–41 | date = September 1977 | pmid = 410587 | doi = 10.1016/0010-7824(77)90022-1 }}</ref>

Returning from the WHO informative sessions, he worked as a postdoctoral fellow at the [[University of Bordeaux]] for 1 year<ref name=":1" /> before continuing his research activities at the University of Edinburgh in September 1977.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />

=== 1977–1981: human reproductive study ===
Despite a short period at WHO, Aitken had the opportunity to consider all the problems that concern human health, particular [[Infertility|infertility issue]], during his time here, which prompted him to pursue research in human reproductive biology.<ref>{{cite web|date=15 November 2012|title=Top science award for sexual health scientist|url=https://www.abc.net.au/am/content/2012/s3633182.htm?site=centralwest|access-date=19 May 2021|website=www.abc.net.au|language=en-AU}}</ref>

In 1977, Aitken had been appointed to the first Medical Research Council Centre for Reproductive Health at University of Edinburgh, where he and his team focused on the [[Implantation (human embryo)|biochemistry of implantation]].<ref name=":2" /> During his early days at the newly founded centre, he found an advanced technique for examining proteins and carbohydrates more precisely during the pre-ovulatory period to study [[Hormone|hormonal control]] of implantation.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Maathuis JB, Aitken RJ | title = Cyclic variation in concentrations of protein and hexose in human uterine flushings collected by an improved technique | language = en-US | journal = Journal of Reproduction and Fertility | volume = 52 | issue = 2 | pages = 289–95 | date = March 1978 | pmid = 633215 | doi = 10.1530/jrf.0.0520289 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Despite early achievements, his team had suspended all research activities due to material shortage from [[Gynaecology|gynaecology wards]].<ref name=":2" />
[[File:Edinburgh Medical School building, Teviot Place.jpg|alt=MRC Centre for Reproductive Health|thumb|[[University of Edinburgh Medical School|Edinburgh Medical School]], where Aitken spent over 25 years doing the reproductive study.]]

=== 1982–1998: initiative in andrology ===
After months of waiting for clinical supplies, Aitken took the lead in [[Andrology]] with Roger Short and [[David Mortimer (andrologist)|David Mortimer]]'s encouragement,<ref name=":2" /> despite the fact that the discipline was still in its infancy around the 1950s.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Isidori A | title = [The history of modern andrology] | journal = Medicina Nei Secoli | volume = 13 | issue = 2 | pages = 255–68 | date = 2001 | pmid = 12374107 }}</ref> With this transition in research styles, he could gain direct access without relying on his clinical colleagues' supply,<ref name=":2" /> thus solving the need for clinical materials. In 1982, he was promoted to senior scientist at the Medical Research Council;<ref name=":1" /> however, it was initially difficult since he and his team were all obscure about how they could influence this field.<ref name=":2" />  After few years with renovated laboratory facilities, Aitken started to focus his future study on clinical research into male contraceptives, androgen physiology, and male infertility, especially molecular mechanisms that regulate sperm function.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Aitken RJ, Irvine DS, Wu FC | title = Prospective analysis of sperm-oocyte fusion and reactive oxygen species generation as criteria for the diagnosis of infertility | journal = American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology | volume = 164 | issue = 2 | pages = 542–51 | date = February 1991 | pmid = 1992700 | doi = 10.1016/s0002-9378(11)80017-7 }}</ref>

Aitken remained at the University of Edinburgh for most of the 1980s to 1990s. It was there that he discovered an abnormally free radical attack in failures of fertilisation<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Aitken RJ, Clarkson JS, Fishel S | title = Generation of reactive oxygen species, lipid peroxidation, and human sperm function | journal = Biology of Reproduction | volume = 41 | issue = 1 | pages = 183–97 | date = July 1989 | pmid = 2553141 | doi = 10.1095/biolreprod41.1.183 | doi-access = free }}</ref> and later did research on the relationship between reactive oxygen species and their effects on impaired sperm function.<ref name="andrology-reactive">{{cite journal |last1=Aitken |first1=R. John |last2=Jones |first2=Keith T. |last3=Robertson |first3=Sarah A. |title=Reactive Oxygen Species and Sperm Function—In Sickness and In Health |journal=Journal of Andrology |date=2012 |volume=33 |issue=6 |pages=1096–1106 |doi=10.2164/jandrol.112.016535|pmid=22879525 |doi-access= }}</ref> He also proposed new techniques in contraception that had helped prevent sexually transmitted diseases and treat male infertility.<ref name=":4">{{cite journal | vauthors = Aitken RJ | title = New techniques in contraception: gossypol, vaccines and GnRH analogues | journal = Proceedings of the Annual Symposium of the Eugenics Society | volume = 19 | pages = 1–18 | date = 1983 | pmid = 6366784 }}</ref> These contributions laid the foundation for the reproductive studies done in the latter half of the twentieth century and later.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Griveau|first1=J. F.|last2=Lannou|first2=D. Le|date=1997|title=Reactive oxygen species and human spermatozoa: physiology and pathology|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1046/j.1365-2605.1997.00044.x|journal=International Journal of Andrology|language=en|volume=20|issue=2|pages=61–69|doi=10.1046/j.1365-2605.1997.00044.x|pmid=9292315|issn=1365-2605|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=":15">{{Cite journal|last=Tremellen|first=Kelton|date=1 May 2008|title=Oxidative stress and male infertility—a clinical perspective|journal=Human Reproduction Update|volume=14|issue=3|pages=243–258|doi=10.1093/humupd/dmn004|pmid=18281241|issn=1355-4786|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==== Oxidative stress ====
During the time at the University of Edinburgh, Aitken worked with multiple antibodies to analyse their effects on fertilisation and human sperm function.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Dor J, Rudak E, Aitken RJ | title = Antisperm antibodies: their effect on the process of fertilization studied in vitro | journal = Fertility and Sterility | volume = 35 | issue = 5 | pages = 535–41 | date = May 1981 | pmid = 7227569 | doi = 10.1016/S0015-0282(16)45496-8 | doi-access =  }}</ref> When he gave the administration of [[A23187]] to spermatozoa from normal fertile and [[oligospermia]], he discovered a decline in fertilisation rates at a higher dose, which reduced sperm motility.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Aitken RJ, Ross A, Hargreave T, Richardson D, Best F | title = Analysis of human sperm function following exposure to the ionophore A23187. Comparison of normospermic and oligozoospermic men | journal = Journal of Andrology | volume = 5 | issue = 5 | pages = 321–9 | date = 10 September 1984 | pmid = 6438035 | doi = 10.1002/j.1939-4640.1984.tb00796.x | doi-access = free }}</ref> In attempt to explain the cellular basis of defective sperm function association in a 1987 paper in the ''[[Journal of Reproduction and Fertility]]'', he found a sudden burst of production of [[Reactive oxygen species|reactive oxygen species (ROS)]] associated with the free radical attack in [[male infertility]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Aitken RJ, Clarkson JS | title = Cellular basis of defective sperm function and its association with the genesis of reactive oxygen species by human spermatozoa | language = en-US | journal = Journal of Reproduction and Fertility | volume = 81 | issue = 2 | pages = 459–69 | date = November 1987 | pmid = 2828610 | doi = 10.1530/jrf.0.0810459 | doi-access =  }}</ref> The hyperactive production of ROS causes [[Lipid peroxidation|peroxidative damage]] to the sperm plasma membrane, which is known as [[oxidative stress]], resulting in loss of sperm function.<ref name=":15" />

The discovery was later acknowledged by thousands of scientists as a foundational concept in studying oxygen species associated pathophysiology.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Moazamian R, Polhemus A, Connaughton H, Fraser B, Whiting S, Gharagozloo P, Aitken RJ | title = Oxidative stress and human spermatozoa: diagnostic and functional significance of aldehydes generated as a result of lipid peroxidation | journal = Molecular Human Reproduction | volume = 21 | issue = 6 | pages = 502–15 | date = June 2015 | pmid = 25837702 | doi = 10.1093/molehr/gav014 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Aitken's paper had expanded on the molecular modifications of oxidants in male infertility and resulted in new therapeutic intervention methods to maintain reproductive function.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Aitken RJ, Clarkson JS | title = Significance of reactive oxygen species and antioxidants in defining the efficacy of sperm preparation techniques | journal = Journal of Andrology | volume = 9 | issue = 6 | pages = 367–76 | date = 1988 | pmid = 3215823 | doi = 10.1002/j.1939-4640.1988.tb01067.x | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Agarwal A, Roychoudhury S, Bjugstad KB, Cho CL | title = Oxidation-reduction potential of semen: what is its role in the treatment of male infertility? | journal = Therapeutic Advances in Urology | volume = 8 | issue = 5 | pages = 302–318 | date = October 2016 | pmid = 27695529 | pmc = 5004233 | doi = 10.1177/1756287216652779 }}</ref>

==== Contraceptive vaccine ====
Besides discovering oxidative stress, Aitken also improved the male [[contraceptive vaccine]] in later years.<ref name=":4" /> His paper in the European Journal of Pharmacology in 1990 proposed 3 possible targets, including [[Human chorionic gonadotropin|hCG]], [[zona pellucida]] and [[Sperm|sperm surface]] for contraception development.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Aitken RJ | date = July 1990 |title=Contraceptive vaccine development |journal=European Journal of Pharmacology|language=en|volume=183|issue=1|pages=13|doi=10.1016/0014-2999(90)91256-B }}</ref> This research provided the foundation for designing a long-lasting and reversible form of contraceptives, providing an effective method to help prevent sexually transmitted diseases and control the world's growing population.<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite web|last=Wallace|first=Natasha|date=25 August 2013|title=Experts hope new contraceptive will cut abortion rates|url=https://www.smh.com.au/healthcare/experts-hope-new-contraceptive-will-cut-abortion-rates-20130825-2skac.html|access-date=31 May 2021|website=The Sydney Morning Herald|language=en}}</ref>

=== 1998–2004: emigration to Australia ===
The University of Cambridge awarded Aitken a [[Doctor of Science|Doctor of Science (ScD)]] in 1998 to recognise his achievements in [[gamete]] biology.<ref name=":13">{{cite web|title=John Aitken|url=https://www.srb.org.au/john-aitken-2|access-date=21 May 2021|website=SRB|language=en-AU}}</ref> At the same time, he got a phone call from the [[University of Newcastle (Australia)|University of Newcastle]], inviting him to take up the Chair of Biological Sciences. He first declined because he mistook Newcastle for [[Newcastle upon Tyne]], but then agreed after learning that the university is in Australia.<ref name=":2" /> It was here that he later took part in several important roles such as Head of School, Director of an ARC Centre of Excellence then Pro-Vice-Chancellor of the Faculty of Health and Medicine at the University of Newcastle.<ref name=":14">{{cite web|date=16 January 2015|title=Staff Profile|url=https://www.newcastle.edu.au/profile/john-aitken|access-date=21 May 2021|website=www.newcastle.edu.au|language=en}}</ref>
[[File:UNew MedSci Building.jpg|thumb|Aitken has been working at [[University of Newcastle (Australia)|University of Newcastle]] since 1998.]]
While serving high positions at the University of Newcastle, Aitken continued his research career on the reproductive studies. He and his colleagues conducted further research on the effects of oxidative stress on the physiological and functional integrity of human sperm.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Twigg J, Fulton N, Gomez E, Irvine DS, Aitken RJ | title = Analysis of the impact of intracellular reactive oxygen species generation on the structural and functional integrity of human spermatozoa: lipid peroxidation, DNA fragmentation and effectiveness of antioxidants | journal = Human Reproduction | volume = 13 | issue = 6 | pages = 1429–36 | date = June 1998 | pmid = 9688366 | doi = 10.1093/humrep/13.6.1429 | doi-access = free }}</ref> They also researched related oxidative stress problems, such as genetic alterations in male infertility, which culminated in [[Gene mutation|gene mutations]], discussing the possible health issues of the next generation from couples using [[assisted reproductive technology]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Aitken RJ, Krausz C | title = Oxidative stress, DNA damage and the Y chromosome | language = en-US | journal = Reproduction | volume = 122 | issue = 4 | pages = 497–506 | date = October 2001 | pmid = 11570956 | doi = 10.1530/rep.0.1220497 | doi-access = free | hdl = 2158/778616 | hdl-access = free }}</ref>

He and his colleagues continued to research safe and reliable contraception vaccinations for controlling human fertility. Their study included developing the potential contraceptive potential of [[ZP3|ZP3 peptides]]<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Paterson M, Wilson MR, Jennings ZA, van Duin M, Aitken RJ | title = Design and evaluation of a ZP3 peptide vaccine in a homologous primate model | journal = Molecular Human Reproduction | volume = 5 | issue = 4 | pages = 342–52 | date = April 1999 | pmid = 10321806 | doi = 10.1093/molehr/5.4.342 | doi-access = free }}</ref> and other chemical compositions of these contraceptive agents, implying the potential effectiveness of the anti-hCG antibodies.<ref name=":5">{{cite journal | vauthors = McLaughlin EA, Holland MK, Aitken RJ | title = Contraceptive vaccines | journal = Expert Opinion on Biological Therapy | volume = 3 | issue = 5 | pages = 829–41 | date = August 2003 | pmid = 12880382 | doi = 10.1517/14712598.3.5.829 | s2cid = 24838026 }}</ref>

During his early years in Australia, Aitken attempted to diverge his studies from human reproductive science.<ref name=":2" /> He released articles that helped identify diseases in various Australian species, including [[tammar wallaby]] and [[brushtail possum]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Sidhu KS, Mate KE, Gunasekera T, Veal D, Hetherington L, Baker MA, Aitken RJ, Rodger JC | display-authors = 6 | title = A flow cytometric assay for global estimation of tyrosine phosphorylation associated with capacitation of spermatozoa from two marsupial species, the tammar wallaby (Macropus eugenii) and the brushtail possum (Trichosurus vulpecula) | language = en-US | journal = Reproduction | volume = 127 | issue = 1 | pages = 95–103 | date = January 2004 | pmid = 15056774 | doi = 10.1530/rep.1.00073 | doi-access = free }}</ref> In addition, he discovered [[Ehrlichia|Ehrlichia platys]] in dogs in Australia, which had not previously been found in Australian animals.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Brown GK, Martin AR, Roberts TK, Aitken RJ | title = Detection of Ehrlichia platys in dogs in Australia | journal = Australian Veterinary Journal | volume = 79 | issue = 8 | pages = 554–8 | date = August 2001 | pmid = 11599817 | doi = 10.1111/j.1751-0813.2001.tb10747.x }}</ref> However, after few years, he decided to return to andrology and the pursuit of understanding the [[cell biology]] of [[Spermatozoon|spermatozoa]].<ref name=":2" />

=== 2005–2018 ===
According to [[Google Scholar]], this is the period where Aitken's papers were receiving an increasing number of citations.<ref>{{cite web|title=Robert John Aitken|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=cJ9WRccAAAAJ|access-date=22 May 2021|website=scholar.google.com}}</ref> During this time, Aitken and his team carried out some studies to identify different causes affecting male reproductive health. They found that environmental conditions such as smoking,<ref name=":6">{{cite journal | vauthors = Aitken RJ, De Iuliis GN | title = Origins and consequences of DNA damage in male germ cells | journal = Reproductive Biomedicine Online | volume = 14 | issue = 6 | pages = 727–33 | date = June 2007 | pmid = 17579989 | doi = 10.1016/s1472-6483(10)60676-1 }}</ref> toxins, and mobile radiation<ref name=":7">{{cite journal | vauthors = Aitken RJ, Bennetts LE, Sawyer D, Wiklendt AM, King BV | title = Impact of radio frequency electromagnetic radiation on DNA integrity in the male germline | journal = International Journal of Andrology | volume = 28 | issue = 3 | pages = 171–9 | date = June 2005 | pmid = 15910543 | doi = 10.1111/j.1365-2605.2005.00531.x | doi-access = free }}</ref> contribute to various health issues. These not simply affect male fertility by causing oxidative stress, but they also cause DNA damage, increasing the risk of a man's children developing infertility or cancer.<ref name=":6" />

Along with the studies on  DNA integrity, the effect of radiofrequency radiation<ref name=":7" /> on [[fertility]], contraceptive<ref name=":5" /> and [[fertility preservation]] in patients, Aitken has been working on [[molecular markers]] of oxidative stress and developing sensitive methods to measure reactive oxygen species generation by cells. Their discovery showed the effectiveness of numerous diagnostic techniques, such as [[Chromatography detector|chemiluminescence]], [[spectrophotometry]], and [[flow cytometry]], as an indicator of oxidative stress, emphasizing the general significance of [[Mitochondrial disease|mitochondrial dysregulation]] in impaired sperm activity.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Aitken RJ, Smith TB, Lord T, Kuczera L, Koppers AJ, Naumovski N, Connaughton H, Baker MA, De Iuliis GN | display-authors = 6 | title = On methods for the detection of reactive oxygen species generation by human spermatozoa: analysis of the cellular responses to catechol oestrogen, lipid aldehyde, menadione and arachidonic acid | journal = Andrology | volume = 1 | issue = 2 | pages = 192–205 | date = March 2013 | pmid = 23316012 | doi = 10.1111/j.2047-2927.2012.00056.x | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Despite not gaining much success in the animal study, his contribution to developing immunocontraception on animals ranging from horses, sub-mammalian organisms to annelid worms, oysters, and fish enabled the development of a nonsurgical sterilization technique. In 2015, he received a patent for his "Method for reducing the Reproductive Potential of an Animal" while working with [[Eileen McLaughlin]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=contact=+61 2 6283 2999|first=scheme=AGLSTERMS AglsAgent; corporateName=IP Australia; address=PO Box 200 Woden ACT 2606|date=1 August 2015|title=Source IP|url=https://sourceip.ipaustralia.gov.au/patent/method-reducing-reproductive-potential-animal-au2015903058/AVEtHvzM5tguNXLCkBf7|access-date=26 May 2021|website=sourceip.ipaustralia.gov.au|language=en}}</ref> His invention revolutionized Australian horse breeding industry, which provided a new method of controlling the horse population and increase their value.<ref>{{Cite web|date=14 November 2012|title=Newcastle scientist honoured for fertility work|url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2012-11-15/newcastle-scientist-honoured-for-fertility-work/4372704|access-date=31 May 2021|website=www.abc.net.au|language=en-AU}}</ref>

=== 2018–current ===
In more recent years, Aitken has been focusing on translational research in male contraception and male infertility. Since 2016, he has been working alongside Memphasis to develop "Felix", a device which uses a patented cell separation technology to more gently and effectively separate sperm from semen samples.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2 June 2020|title='Felix' to transform fertility for millions of couples worldwide|url=https://www.newcastle.edu.au/newsroom/faculty-of-science/felix-to-transform-fertility-for-millions-of-couples-worldwide|access-date=26 May 2021|website=The University of Newcastle, Australia|language=en}}</ref> This project seeks to increase the collection of vital, stable sperm during the crucial early stages of the IVF process.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hydrix and Memphasys awarded 2020 Good Design Awards for the Felix™ ART/IVF technology|url=https://www.hydrix.com/news-articles/hydrix-wins-good-design-awards|access-date=31 May 2021|website=www.hydrix.com|date=9 September 2020 |language=en}}</ref>

== Awards and honours ==

=== Awards ===

* 1986–87: Walpole Prize for fertility research, Society for Reproduction and Fertility<ref name=":12" />
* 2006: Faculty Award for Research Excellence, University of Newcastle<ref name=":14" />
* 2011: Excellence in Innovation, University of Newcastle<ref name=":14" />
* 2012: NSW Scientist of the Year<ref>{{cite web|title=Honour Roll – NSW Chief Scientist & Engineer|url=http://www.chiefscientist.nsw.gov.au/premiersprizes/previous-winners|access-date=20 March 2018|website=www.chiefscientist.nsw.gov.au|language=en|archive-date=14 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200814204702/https://www.chiefscientist.nsw.gov.au/premiersprizes/previous-winners|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* 2016: Carl G. Hartman Award, Society for the Study of Reproduction, USA<ref>{{cite web|title=Carl G. Hartman Award|url=http://www.ssr.org/HartmanAward|website=www.ssr.org|access-date=20 March 2018|language=en|date=16 August 2013}}</ref>
* 2021: Clarke Medal, Royal Society of New South Wales<ref>{{Cite web |title=Clarke Medal |url=https://www.royalsoc.org.au/awards/clarke-medal |access-date=2022-08-03 |website=The Royal Society of NSW|date=21 August 2015 }}</ref>

=== Membership in professional societies ===

* 1995–present: Fellow – [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]]<ref name=":8" />
* 2011–present: Fellow – [[Australian Academy of Science]]<ref name=":9" />
* 2015–present: Fellow – [[Australian Academy of Health and Medical Sciences]]<ref name=":10" />
* 2003–2010: Director – [[Australian Research Council|ARC Centre of Excellence in Biotechnology and Development]]<ref name=":13" /><ref name=":14" />
* 2003–2010: Co-director – Priority Research Centre in Reproductive Science, University of Newcastle<ref name=":14" />
* 2012–2017: President – International Society of Andrology<ref name=":11" />
* 2014 - present: Fellow - [[Royal Society of New South Wales]] (Est 1821) promulgated by HE the Governor in the NSW Government Gazette February 2018, Chair of the Hunter Branch (2022-24).

== Other interests ==
Aitken's cultural interests go beyond science.<ref name=":0" /> 

=== Music ===
Before deciding to pursue a career as a scientist, music was his greatest passion.<ref name=":0" /> He played the guitar most of the time during his time at the University of London and joined the university's folk music club. He loved the music of [[Frank Sinatra]], [[Nelson Riddle Orchestra]] and especially [[Bob Dylan]].<ref name=":0" />
